subject: Banking
title: Wirecard: Germany's Banking Fraud
description: A quick, practical guide to Wirecard: Germany's Banking Fraud.

hook.text: Wirecard was a German fintech darling worth $28 billion.

buildup.text: Wirecard processed payments for online merchants. It claimed rapid growth in Asia.

discovery.text: The $2.1 billion was supposedly held in Philippine bank accounts. The banks confirmed the accounts didn't exist.

twist.text: Germany's financial regulator BaFin had investigated whistleblowers who reported fraud.

climax.text: Wirecard proved that regulators can be fooled by national champions.

punchline.text: $2.1 billion that never existed. Regulators investigated whistleblowers instead.

quiz.question: What was unique about Wirecard's fraud?
options: $2.1 billion in reported cash simply did not exist in any account
It was only detected by AI

details.summary: Wirecard fabricated $2.1 billion in cash that never existed, fooling auditor EY and Germany's financial regulator BaFin for years. The 2020 collapse was Europe's largest corporate fraud and a catastrophic failure of German financial oversight.
details.whyItMatters: Wirecard exposed the weakness of trusting auditors and regulators to catch fraud. Germany's financial regulator actively protected the company from journalists and short sellers who correctly identified the fraud years earlier.
takeaways: Wirecard claimed $2.1 billion in cash held in Philippine bank accounts that did not exist
Auditor EY failed to directly verify bank balances for years
BaFin banned short selling of Wirecard shares and reported journalists to prosecutors

faq.question: How did Wirecard get away with fraud for so long?
faq.answer: Wirecard exploited Germany's national pride in having a tech champion. BaFin treated skeptics as market manipulators, EY trusted third-party confirmations instead of verifying directly, and investors ignored red flags raised by Financial Times journalists.

faq.question: What happened to Wirecard's former CEO?
faq.answer: CEO Markus Braun was arrested and charged with fraud. COO Jan Marsalek, believed to have masterminded the scheme, fled and is reportedly in Russia. The ongoing trial is one of the largest corporate fraud cases in European history.
